newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Looking for spread narrowing.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Looking for spread narrowing.

text.p: Gilts face a barrage of data this week but should end up in better shape, with the spread over Bunds having widened to enticing levels, analysts said on Monday.
With Monday's producer prices providing no surprises, the market will look to Wednesday's jobs figures and the following day's retail price data for direction.
But with the gilt/Bund spread above 170 basis points for the first time in about five weeks, it will take some pretty extreme figures to force the UK into further underperformance.
"With the spread back over 170 against Bunds there will be trades out of the German market, back into gilts," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW.

But although a move back into the 150s was justified by the fundamentals, Adams said the fact that the spread of 10-year gilt yields over their U.S. counterparts is now just 100 basis points, its lowest level since early 1995, could constrain the UK market.
Mark Hale, economist at Sakura Finance, also saw some scope for outperformance over most European bond markets.
"The UK and Denmark are relatively safe havens...not affected by the likely rows over European Monetary Union, with both countries having an opt-out," he said on Reuters Financial Television.

August producer prices proved an easy pill for the market to swallow, with output prices flat on the month and up 2.0 percent year-on-year, input prices up 0.3 percent on the month but still 2.2 percent below their year-ago level.
Year-on-year output price inflation is now at its lowest level since July 1994, while year-on-year core output prices are at their lowest level in nearly 30 years.
"They confirm very modest producer price inflation...but we do not expect the rest of the week's inflation news to be as encouraging," said Marian Bell, economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland.

She forecast underlying retail price inflation to hold stubbornly at 2.8 percent year-on-year -- the consensus is for it to edge down to 2.7 -- and said there was a risk of underlying average earnings growth rising to 4.0 percent.
Most economists expect earnings growth to stay put at an annualised 3.75 percent in July. Unemployment is forecast to fall by an above-trend 15,000 in August.
"A tightening labour market is seen as okay as long as it doesn't feed through to wage pressures," Adams at BZW said. "That means average earnings will be this week's key figure."
In terms of curve plays, flattening should be the order of the week, analysts said, with hopes of interest rate cuts receding but benign inflation indicators comforting the longer end of the curve.

Analysts at Merrill Lynch said the gilt yield curve between two and 10-years is at its steepest since more than three years ago, when the aftermath of Britain's exit from the European Exchange Rate Mechanism buffeted the gilt market.

"Present circumstances, although complicated by the looming general election, are not nearly so volatile," they said in a client note. "In our view, the steepness of the yield curve should not be so sharp."

Like Adams at BZW, the Merrill analysts said the gilt/T-note spread was as narrow as it will get. "While we remain bullish on the gilt market over the longer term, we think it unlikely a spread below 100 basis points can be maintained in the short-term."
